tweets.text: A lending protocol that values collateral with a price an attacker can move is making decisions on incorrect values. That is price oracle manipulation, listed by OWASP as SC03.

The root cause is trust. A contract implicitly assumes the price reflects market conditions, so the oracle becomes a trust boundary. Manipulation, staleness or misconfiguration can violate that trust.
Spot price manipulation can come from large trades, flash loans or just-in-time liquidity in the same block. If core prices read a single spot value, the attacker only needs to move that one input.
TWAPs are not automatically safe. OWASP lists TWAP manipulation over short windows or low-liquidity periods, plus stale or stuck data when freshness is not enforced.
Aggregation can fail too. If it does not reject outliers, one manipulated source can still skew the result.
Mitigation starts with inputs: aggregate multiple sources with a median or mean and reject outliers. Use TWAPs over sufficient windows and reject prices older than a maximum staleness threshold.
Limit exposure to any single source. Avoid basing core prices on illiquid pools, and cap the impact of a single pool or feed.
When data looks suspicious or is unavailable, halt sensitive operations such as borrowing and liquidations. Also monitor deviations between the oracle and reference markets with automated alerts.
Check your own contract: which price inputs can an attacker move, directly or indirectly? Is freshness enforced, are outliers rejected, and what pauses when the price feed fails?

tweets.text: A withdrawal that sends Ether before clearing the caller balance can be withdrawn against again and again, because the balance is still unchanged when control comes back.
The mechanism: calling another contract hands it control. It can call back before the first call returns. State updates that come after an untrusted call allow repeated execution.
In the withdrawal case, the callback runs while the stored balance has not been cleared yet. So the second withdrawal is checked against the same old balance as the first.
Ether transfers are not the only way in. Reentrancy can arise from calls to other contracts too, and dependencies across multiple contracts also matter.
The fix is checks-effects-interactions: validate inputs and permissions, update the relevant storage state, then make external calls.
For the withdrawal, save the amount and clear the stored balance before calling the recipient, as in `balances[msg.sender] = 0;` placed ahead of the external call.
Then require the call to succeed, so a failure reverts the whole operation instead of leaving state half finished.
A callback may enter through another function or dependency, not just the one you are reading. Review other callable paths and contracts that share the affected state.
Closing check for your own code: in each function, does any external call happen before the storage it depends on is updated? And which other paths share that state?

tweets.text: An empty ERC-4626 vault, a 1 unit deposit and a direct token transfer to the vault can leave the next depositor with zero shares. The attacker then redeems for the vault's whole balance.
The root cause is the share price. A donation sent straight to the vault mints no shares, so the attacker's single share is now worth everything in the vault.

Consider a victim depositing 100 tokens into a new vault. The attacker front-runs with 1 wei for one share, then transfers 100 tokens or more directly to the vault. The vault balance now looks like 101 tokens backing one share.

The victim's 100 tokens divide by 101 and round down to zero shares under Solidity integer division. The attacker redeems the single share and takes the full 101 token balance, including the victim's deposit.
No access control bug is needed. The vault in that example reads its live token balance with `balanceOf(address(this))`, so a plain transfer shifts the exchange rate without calling deposit.
OpenZeppelin's fix uses virtual shares and assets with a decimal offset. The rate becomes `totalAssets() + 1` over `totalSupply() + 10**offset`, so even an empty vault has a defined rate.
The offset raises the donation an attacker needs by that many orders of magnitude. The virtual shares also capture part of the donation, which sets a high price for inflating the rate.
Other mitigations: dead shares minted to an unrecoverable address at deployment, an initial deposit made atomically at deploy, and minimum share checks that revert a deposit receiving too few shares.
The risk is highest when a vault is empty or nearly empty, such as at launch or after everyone withdraws. Any protocol that reads a vault's share price as a price can be manipulated the same way.
Before trusting a vault, check how it computes `totalAssets()`, whether it uses virtual shares or seeds an initial deposit, and whether deposits revert on too few shares. Does yours do all three?
